frontmatter.title: 1. Tuning in
frontmatter.subtitle: Sensing, sound, and music across musicology, psychology, and technology

children.value: This first chapter explains the words used in the course name (
), and why combining perspectives from musicology, psychology, and technology is useful.
This course is called “Sensing Sound and Music”. But what does that mean? And what do those three words mean on their own?
Can you define the three terms “sensing”, “sound”, and “music”?
Sound and music run through almost everything humans do, both as a way of communicating and as an art form.
is a physical phenomenon: vibrations travelling through a medium.
is sound that has been organised so that it carries emotional, cognitive, and cultural meaning. We

sound through the auditory system, but, as the course will show, also through the body. Exactly how we sense music is still one of the open questions in music psychology and it also has deep implications for music technology.
Levels of description: from physics to interpretation
Throughout the course it helps to keep in mind that we discuss sound and music at several levels. They are connected but they are not the same thing:

: Pressure waves in air (and in solids or liquids) obey acoustics: frequency–wavelength relationships, reflection, diffraction, and how instruments and rooms shape spectra and timing. This is the world microphones capture and loudspeakers re‑radiate. See
: Once transduced (converted into an electrical signal), sound becomes

: voltages, then numbers. Sampling, quantisation, filtering, compression, and synthesis all operate here. The representation is always partial, and the choices made when digitising affect what can be recovered or analysed later. See

: The ear and early auditory processing turn waveforms into what we distinguish as pitch, loudness, timbre, and location, often in ways that diverge from simple physics (masking, streaming, illusions). See
: Expectation, memory, attention, culture, and affect colour what sounds
, whether as speech, music, warning, or ambience. Bodily states and neural circuits studied in psychology and neuroscience link to how we attend to and evaluate sound over time. See

children.alt: four boxes labelled air, file, ear and mind, joined by arrows; the first two bracketed as measured by a device, the last two as experienced by a person

children.value: The four levels of description as four words to remember: air, file, ear, mind. The first two can be measured with a device; the last two need a person.

These four levels are the “spine” of the course. Each chapter from here on opens by saying which of them it works at, so that you always know whether a claim is about the air, the file, the ear, or the mind. It is easy to mix them up in discussion, that is why you should think about the differences from the start. We can record and measure sound with a microphone at the
. At the end of the course, you will have a much more solid understanding of how the different levels relate to each other and a vocabulary to speak about the differences.

. It draws on methods, theories, and perspectives from several fields to ask questions about sound and music. Interdisciplinarity is more than putting different kinds of knowledge side by side; here it means genuinely combining musicology, psychology, and technology. Looking at sound and music from these different angles tells us more about how people perceive, experience, and create music, and about how technology shapes those processes.
The three can also be drawn another way, and the book keeps that drawing in the background. Musicology in a broad sense, the study of

(introduced later in this chapter), is the centre: everything in the course is about what people do with sound and music. Psychology and technology are then two ways into that centre, and the third, which has no chapter of its own but runs through all of them, is

, the careful description of experience. Each time the book asks you to stand up, close your eyes and listen, it is asking for that. The four levels above sort themselves among the three: technology works in the air and the file, psychology in the ear, and phenomenology in the mind.
is the scientific study of the origin and history of words and how their meanings and forms have changed over time. The word “etymology” is itself derived from the Ancient Greek words
, meaning “true sense or sense of a truth”, and the suffix
, denoting “the study or logic of”. Similarly, we can investigate the three disciplines in question:
: The term “musicology” comes from the Greek words

(study). It is the scholarly study of music, covering its history, theory, and cultural context. Musicologists analyse how music is composed, performed, and understood across different societies and eras.
(study). It is the scientific study of the mind and behaviour. Music psychologists explore how people perceive, process, and respond to music emotionally and cognitively.
: The word “technology” originates from the Greek

(study). Strictly, then, technology is the study of the craft, and the craft itself, with its tools and methods, is technique. Everyday English has let the word swallow both meanings; German and Norwegian keep them apart (
), and this book follows that where it can:
for the devices and the means,

for the field that studies and develops them. Music technology, in that sense, is the development and study of instruments, recording devices, software, and other inventions that help create, analyse, or experience music.
By the end of the course, you will have learned some of the basic terminology, theories, and methods used in all these directions.
Can you think of other words with a “logy” at the end? What do they mean?
Disciplines can work together in several ways, and many people call all of them “interdisciplinarity”. There are differences, and the figure shows five of them:
An illustration of different levels of disciplinarity, from
work looks at one discipline from the point of view of another.
work puts people from several disciplines side by side, each using their own expertise.
work joins the knowledge and methods of several disciplines into one approach.
work goes further and builds a shared framework that no single discipline owns.

None of these is better than the others, and the same researcher may play different roles in different projects. It helps to know which one a project attempts when we look at how each discipline combines theories and methods.
How do you define your own background in terms of disciplinarity?

A discipline holds together through its concepts, theories, and methods, and through shared traditions, a vocabulary, and agreed standards for what counts as good work. Journals, conferences, and professional organisations keep these alive. What a discipline treats as its territory follows from its history, its core questions, and the problems it has taken on.

Each of the three disciplines in this course brings its own theories and methods. Roughly speaking, musicology uses analysis, historiography, and ethnography; psychology runs experiments and surveys; and technology builds on engineering and computational modelling. Once you read the literature and follow how the fields developed, the picture is less tidy. None of them grew in a straight line, and they become more entangled the more they are mixed.

Most people have not met music psychology or music technology as academic disciplines. Musicology is a little more familiar, since schools usually teach some of its basics: Western music theory, notation, and music history. The chapter on
picks up that thread after acoustics and psychoacoustics, and connects
to the symbols you may already use in analysis. First, some fundamentals of each discipline.
Music psychology studies how people perceive, process, and respond to sound and music. Its main topics:
: how the ear and the brain turn sound into pitch, loudness, timbre, rhythm, and location.
: the mental work of making sense of music: memory, expectation, attention, and finding patterns and boundaries.
: how music evokes, expresses, and regulates feelings, in the mind and in the body.
: how music makes us move and interact, from tapping and dancing to playing together and bonding.
: how musical abilities and tastes grow and change through life, from infancy to expertise.
In this course, we will primarily investigate perception, and briefly touch on cognition and behaviour.
The field has its own societies, conferences, and journals:
Conferences and Communities in Music Psychology
ESCOM (European Society for the Cognitive Sciences of Music)
: A society that organises conferences and promotes research in the cognitive sciences of music.
ICMPC (International Conference on Music Perception and Cognition)
: A biennial conference that brings together researchers from around the world to discuss music perception and cognition.
SMPC (Society for Music Perception and Cognition)
: A society that hosts conferences and fosters research on the psychological and cognitive aspects of music.
: A conference dedicated to the intersection of neuroscience and music, exploring topics such as music perception, cognition, and therapy.
: A leading journal that publishes research on the perception and cognition of music, including studies on auditory processing, musical memory, and emotional responses.
: Explores the intersection of music psychology, technology, and theory, with an emphasis on computational and experimental approaches.
: Publishes empirical studies on music perception, cognition, and performance, as well as reviews of current research.
: Covers a wide range of topics in music psychology, including music education, therapy, and cultural studies.
: A general-purpose journal with a section that focuses on auditory perception, music cognition, and related neuroscience.
: An interdisciplinary journal that publishes research on the scientific study of music, including its psychological, cultural, and technological dimensions.
: The journal of the European Society for the Cognitive Sciences of Music, publishing research on music psychology, cognition, perception, and interdisciplinary studies.

Music psychology sits between fields. Its researchers usually work in either a musicology or a psychology department, and that shapes the research. Those in musicology departments tend to study music as it happens in real life, often with qualitative methods, and they value what is called
. Those in psychology departments tend to run controlled experiments with quantitative methods.
Many music psychologists are therefore the only one in their department. A few larger centres gather the whole field under one roof, with all its theories and methods.
at the University of Oslo is one of them.
Many people think of music technology as the products that come out of it. But music technology, the “logy” of
, is also a discipline of its own. It creates, uses, and reflects on tools and systems for making, analysing, and manipulating sound. Its main areas:

: generating and modelling sound (additive, subtractive, FM, wavetable, granular) and taking it apart again (spectral analysis, resynthesis). Used in instrument and sound design, and in research on timbre.

: capturing, editing, mixing, and transforming audio in a DAW. Typical tasks are multitrack recording, filtering and equalisation, compression, reverb and delay, pitch shifting and time stretching, and mastering.
: extracting musical information from audio and scores by computer, often with machine learning. Used for recommendation systems, analysis, and musicology.

: real-time systems for performance and interaction, built from sensors and controllers, mappings, and protocols such as MIDI and OSC. Used in digital instruments, live coding, installations, and adaptive performance systems.
Music technology researchers work in departments of musicology, engineering, or informatics. Many combine artistic exploration with scientific inquiry.
The field also has its own conferences and journals:
Conferences and Communities in Music Technology
: The oldest conference in the field focuses on computer music research, composition, and performance, bringing together artists, scientists, and technologists.
: Covers topics in sound and music computing, including audio analysis, synthesis, and interactive systems.
: Explores new musical instruments and interfaces, emphasising innovation in music performance and interaction.
: Promotes multidisciplinary research in computer music, including psychology, acoustics, and engineering.
: Focuses on the use of sound to convey information, covering topics such as sonification and auditory interfaces.
: Dedicated to research on digital audio effects, signal processing, and music technology.
ISMIR (International Society for Music Information Retrieval)
: Advances research in music information retrieval, including audio analysis, machine learning, and music data processing.

: An international organisation for audio engineers, hosting conferences on sound recording, processing, and reproduction. (The industry keeps its traditional term; by the levels above, what a recording stores is audio, so audio recording is the more precise term.)
: Focuses on digital audio, sound synthesis, and computer-assisted composition, providing insights into the intersection of music and technology.
Journal of the Audio Engineering Society (JAES)
: Covers a wide range of topics in audio engineering, including sound recording, processing, and reproduction.
: Explores the theory and practice of electroacoustic music and sound art, with an emphasis on innovative approaches.
: Publishes research on music technology, computational musicology, and the development of new musical tools and systems.
: Focuses on the creative use of technology in music and sound art, highlighting experimental and interdisciplinary work.
Frontiers in Digital Humanities: Digital Musicology
: Explores the application of digital tools and methods to music analysis, composition, and performance.
Transactions of the International Society for Music Information Retrieval (TISMIR)
: Publishes research on music information retrieval, covering topics such as audio analysis, machine learning, and music data processing.
Even though this course tries to unite psychology and technology, the two differ in kind. Music psychology is a
field. It asks how people perceive, process, and respond to music, and answers with experiments, data, and theory. It looks both for general principles and for how individuals differ.

Music technology is broader. It spans science, art, design, and engineering: research on sound and audio processing, composition and performance, the design of instruments and interfaces, and the building of hardware and software. A music technologist may develop a tool for making music, analyse audio, design an installation, or explore what digital media make possible. Music technology is therefore not only scientific inquiry but also creative practice, invention, and design for users.

At the University of Oslo, we have long combined the two. Advanced technology helps psychological inquiry, and psychological insight shapes how new technology is developed and used. Together they help us understand music as a whole.
After getting introduced to some of the (inter)disciplinary foundations for this course, let us go back to some basics:

. We will spend next week’s class only on listening, but we will start with a little warm-up here. After all, listening is an essential human capacity and central to music, and to psychology and technology. However, most people do not think much about listening in daily life, except for when it is annoying. With a sound level too low, it is hard to hear what is said; with a sound level too loud, it is unpleasant and even dangerous. But why is that, and how do we talk about it in precise terms? That is what we will explore both here and later in class.
Stand up. Close your eyes. Listen. What do you hear?
Let us start with the difference between hearing and listening. We will take
to be the passive, physiological business of detecting sound waves through the auditory system, and
to be the active, cognitive business of interpreting those sounds and making meaning of them.
In the psychology literature, and in
in particular, you will find lists of different types of hearing and listening:
: This occurs when sounds are registered by the ears and processed by the brain without conscious attention. For example, background noise in a café or the hum of an air conditioner.
: The ability to focus on specific sounds or voices while ignoring others, such as following a conversation in a noisy environment (also known as the
: Engaging attention and intention to understand, analyse, or respond to sounds or speech. This matters in music appreciation, communication, and learning.
: Evaluating and analysing sound quality, musical structure, or meaning, often used in music production, performance, or academic study.
: Focusing on the emotional content and intent behind sounds or speech, important in social interactions and therapeutic contexts.

The mechanisms behind these kinds of hearing and listening are still under active investigation, and opinions diverge on how exactly they differ, overlap, or connect. The distinctions are still useful. They give us a vocabulary for the move from automatic sensory processing to deliberate engagement and interpretation.
The view of human psychology in this book is not neutral (no book’s is, even when it pretends otherwise). It grows out of
, which stresses the role of the body in musical experience. Marc Leman did not coin the term, but it became widely known after his book of the same name
Embodied music cognition looked radical at first and has since become fairly mainstream. Researchers at the University of Oslo, starting with professor (now-emeritus)
, have helped develop this line of work over the last few decades. It underpins the studies of music-related body motion in the
and much of what goes on at
The core idea of embodied music cognition is that producing and perceiving music involve sensory, motor, and emotional dimensions at once. To paraphrase
: you explore the world with eyes in a head on a body that moves around. Gibson was mainly interested in vision, but his thinking has shaped how others approach the rest of the senses.
A related idea is that of
argued that music is best understood as a verb—to music—rather than a noun

. Music is not an object, like a song or a score, but something people do. When a band plays a concert, the musicians, the dancers, the audience, the sound engineers, even the people selling tickets and cleaning the hall, are all musicking. Researchers in music education and therapy like the term because it lets them treat music as a social activity rather than a thing: you no longer study “the music” in isolation, but the whole web of musical interaction, from the actions of a performer to the way an audience synchronises its bodies to a beat.
Musicking says that everyone at the concert takes part, but not how. The
sorts musical engagement along two axes
: making music or taking it in. The other runs from

: doing it while the music sounds, or before and after. That gives four kinds of engagement, each with a role: composing (the composer) and performing (the performer) on the creation side, perceiving (the perceiver) and analysing (the analyst) on the experience side. In a traditional concert the four follow each other in a circle, from the composer’s idea through the performance to the people experiencing it, and on to the critic or the student who thinks it over and feeds the next piece. In a band that writes, plays, and listens back to its own recordings, one person may take all four roles in a single evening.

children.alt: four circles labelled composing, performing, perceiving and analysing, with creation below, experience above, out of time to the left and in time to the right, joined by arrows in a circle

children.value: The musicking quadrant: creation and experience, in time and out of time, and the four roles, after
The quadrant is obviously a simplification of a complex reality, but it may help in structuring your thoughts.

are the two in-time roles, and the pair appears often in the chapters on the body, physiology, and vision. A perceiver experiences music with the whole body, not only the ears, which is why the book says
. A listener, in this book, attends to sound through hearing alone. An
is anyone who thinks about music out of time, including when you listen to a recording again for an assignment.

is a tricky one. In psychology it names a particular stage, where the ear and the early auditory system turn a wave into pitch, loudness, and timbre. That is the third level of description above, and the topic of the psychoacoustics chapter. In the quadrant,
names a whole kind of engagement, with attention, memory, and movement included. When this book says perception on its own, it means the psychological level; for the activity, it says experience.

The two frames (levels and quadrant) presented here answer different questions. The levels say what kind of thing a claim is about: the air, the file, the ear, or the mind. The quadrant says what kind of musical engagement is being studied, and by whom. A study of how drummers keep time together is about in-time creation, at the levels of perception and interpretation. A study of how a streaming service tags recordings is about out-of-time analysis, at the digital level. Keeping both in view is a habit worth building from the start.

famously argued that “music is organised sound”. This was his starting point for moving beyond melody and harmony, exploring noise and timbre as compositional material. Music is any sound deliberately shaped and structured over time.
In this course we widen the idea further. We treat music as inherently
. We—like other animals—perceive and make sense of the world through several senses at once, not through hearing alone.
The primary human senses, their associated sensory modalities, and the organs involved in each

For psychologists, multimodality is about how the brain combines information from these channels into a single experience. In music, the clearest case is the link between hearing and body movement. A performer’s visible movements change how we hear their sound, and our own movements feed into how we understand it. But the other senses take part too. Touch gives instrumentalists and singers feedback on what they are doing; proprioception and balance help musicians coordinate posture and motion, especially in dance and performance; and smell or taste can colour the emotional context and memory of a musical event.
Most people would agree that sound is at the heart of music, yet there are striking cases of musicians who have made music with severe hearing loss.
kept composing major works after becoming profoundly deaf, leaning on vision and touch, and the percussionist
performs by feeling vibrations through her hands, feet, and body. How touch and vibration carry musical information is explored in
Beyond combining sight and sound, experiments often turn up systematic

: many perceivers agree that, for example, higher pitches go with brighter lights or smaller shapes.  Many such mappings are well-known and often used in film and game scoring. Such correspondences are not the same as
, which are specific and consistent connections experienced by some (few) individuals.
The simplest demonstration of a crossmodal correspondence needs no laboratory. Look at the two shapes below and decide which is called
. Nearly everyone, in what is known as the

, gives the rounded shape the name with the rounded vowels and soft consonants, and the spiky shape the name with the hard consonants and the high vowel. The choice holds across languages and cultures, including speakers whose writing systems have no letters shaped like the words
. The pairing was first reported by the Gestalt psychologist
, and it was revived under its present name by Ramachandran and Hubbard, who read it as a link between the shape of the mouth in speaking, the acoustic shape of the sound, and the visual shape

. For music the point is that the shape of a sound is not a metaphor perceivers have to learn: a sharp attack and a bright spectrum feel spiky, and a slow attack and a dark spectrum feel round, before any words are attached. That is one reason timbre words such as sharp, round, bright, and dark travel so easily between languages, and it returns when timbre is described in

    "font.size": 10,

theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 720)
# a rounded blob: a circle with a few slow, gentle bulges
round_r = 1 + 0.18 * np.sin(3 * theta + 0.6) + 0.10 * np.sin(5 * theta + 2.0)
# a spiky star: sharp peaks from an absolute-value sawtooth
spiky_r = 0.55 + 0.6 * np.abs(np.sin(5.5 * theta)) ** 3

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
for ax, r, label in zip(axes, [spiky_r, round_r], ["A", "B"]):
    ax.fill(r * np.cos(theta), r * np.sin(theta), color="steelblue")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.4, 1.4)
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(label)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Say the two words aloud and notice what your mouth does. Then, with your voice or an instrument, make one sound that goes with shape A and one that goes with shape B.

Reflect: What did you change between the two sounds, the attack, the pitch, the loudness, or the timbre? Which of those changes would a perceiver who does not know the words still pair with the right shape?
Joint timing between people—such as in ensemble playing, choral breathing, dancing together—returns from an embodied angle in the chapter on

The last concept for this week is the

. The general claim of embodied cognition is that we sense through action and act through sensing. In music, you can see this whenever someone plays an instrument. The sound they hear shapes the next thing they do, and what they do shapes the next sound. A pianist adjusts their touch in response to the tone just produced, and round it goes.

children.alt: a circle between action and perception

children.value: The action–perception loop is at the core of embodied music cognition.
The action–perception loop is also called
. Neither is right or wrong, it is a loop, after all. Which term do you prefer?
puts the action–perception loop at the centre of his idea of
, drawing together psychology, musicology, and acoustic ecology to ask how we engage with sound in everyday life. In his book
he sets out three listening modes:
: Listeners perceive sounds in relation to their environment without needing extensive cognitive processing.
: Sounds provide cues about actions or interactions possible within a given environment.
: The meaning of sounds is shaped by their environmental and situational context.

Clarke also points out that we often hear sounds as “the sound of” something: “the sound of a guitar”, “the sound of a scream”. This source-based listening sits neatly within his three modes: identifying the source is direct perception, hearing what it lets you do is affordance, and reading its situational meaning is contextual listening. Attributing sounds to objects or events is one of the most common ways we make sense of what we hear, and it is one of several listening perspectives we pick up next week.
A critical look: the Mozart effect

children.label: A critical look: the Mozart effect

children.value: Critical thinking is a key skill to develop as a student. You need to learn how to read research results and make up your mind about how solid its conclusions are. Let us discuss one famous claim that made headlines some years ago. Each chapter of this book ends with a section like this one: a claim that many people know, checked against the evidence. The
is the popular idea that listening to
makes you more intelligent. In the 1990s it sold recordings and toys, and the US state of Georgia even funded classical CDs for newborns based on its claims.
reported that college students performed better on a spatial reasoning task after ten minutes of a Mozart sonata than after relaxation instructions or silence.

was thin: 36 participants, one laboratory session, and an advantage that faded within about fifteen minutes. Nothing was measured about general intelligence, about children, or about long-term listening.
was a standard psychology experiment, and it invited replication. Many groups tried, and most found little or nothing.
pooled nearly forty studies with over three thousand participants in a

. The remaining effect was small, appeared after any enjoyable stimulus, and was inflated by selective publication of positive results. Short-lived arousal and mood explain the data better than anything specific to Mozart.
The lesson is not that music does nothing, but that a claim, its evidence, and its method have to be read together. The reading checklist in the

are defined for the course; why musicology, psychology, and technology each offer partial but complementary views; and how interdisciplinarity, listening modes, embodiment, multimodality, and the action–perception loop connect everyday musical activity to the topics that follow. Two frames return throughout: the four levels of description, from the air to the mind, and the musicking quadrant, with creation and experience, in time and out of time. A critical look at the Mozart effect showed why a claim, its evidence, and its method need to be read together.
How do the three pillars of this course—musicology, psychology, and technology—each contribute to understanding sound and music, and what are the risks of staying inside a single discipline?
What are the four levels of description from physical signal to interpretation, and why does it matter to know which level a claim is about?
Where in the musicking quadrant would you place a DJ set, a music critic, and a person humming on the bus, and which levels of description would a study of each need?
What is the action–perception loop, and how might you observe it in a concrete musical situation you know?
In the Mozart effect case, what exactly did the original experiment show, and how did the later meta-analysis change the picture?
